records.p: The dark gray upperparts and barred lower body distinguish the Koch’s cuckooshrike from lighter related forms (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Cuckooshrike is reported from Mindanao and Basilan, and from Samar, Leyte and Bohol under the subspecies boholensis. These forms were formerly included within Coracina striata, and some older records remain difficult to assign under the revised species limits (Clements Checklist, 2024; Wild Bird Club of the Philippines, 2025). Early collectors reported insect and fruit material in individuals examined (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Cuckooshrike is associated with forests. The Clements 2024 revision distinguished Coracina kochii from the former Bar-bellied Cuckooshrike complex using vocal, morphological and mitochondrial characters; it tentatively included the boholensis population (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2024).

records.p: Male plumage has a glossy black face and throat, slate-gray body and paler pearl-gray rump; the female is mostly gray (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-bibbed Cicadabird occurs on Mindanao and Basilan, where the nominate form is recognized, and on Samar, Leyte, Bohol and nearby islands under the subspecies ripleyi. Some older observation datasets use Coracina mindanensis; those records need taxon-concept reconciliation before their mapped localities are transferred to the current Edolisoma combination (Avibase, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). Early examined birds contained fruit and seeds (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-bibbed Cicadabird is associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

In the southern Philippine form historically called Lalage minor, males show a sharply contrasting black-and-white pattern, with a dark, glossy head and upperparts against extensive white on the lower back and underparts. Females are more grey or brownish and show barring on the flanks; McGregor noted geographically varying female throat and chest markings. These southern comparisons should not be generalized to the nominate form across the species range (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-and-white Triller has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Agusan del Sur, and Sultan Kudarat. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Black-and-white Triller is broadly associated with forests.

Adult males show glossy black upperparts, white underparts and a bold white eyebrow; females are greyer above (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pied Triller is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). Forages at several heights in trees, especially the canopy, taking insects and some small fruit (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

An almost uniform light-gray back contrasts with a black facial mask and breast, gray belly and white wing markings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The McGregor's Cuckooshrike has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, South Cotabato, and Sarangani (Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The McGregor's Cuckooshrike is broadly associated with forests. The Mt. Melibengoy authors specifically identified this cuckooshrike among bird taxa warranting additional natural-history and taxonomic study; they did not formally diagnose a new lineage (Pitogo et al., 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Males show a dark hindcrown, pale face, white underparts and slate-grey back; females have a greyer head (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Ashy Minivet has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Ashy Minivet forages high in woodland trees and also visits wooded parks during migration (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adult males have crimson underside and wing patches contrasting with black upperparts; females replace crimson with bright yellow (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Scarlet Minivet is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Scarlet Minivet forages in small groups within the upper forest canopy (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Mindanao Tailor Warbler has a cinnamon-rufous crown, sides of the head and throat, olive-green upperparts, and canary-yellow breast and belly. Its dark wing feathers are edged olive-green. The original description was not assigned to a known sex, so the account does not presume that the plumage is identical in both sexes (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-headed Tailorbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Rufous-headed Tailorbird is broadly associated with forests.

Both sexes of the Yellow-quilled Leafbird were described as predominantly grass-green, darker above, with light yellow on the lores, eye-ring, cheeks and chin. Parts of the flight feathers are edged chamois-yellow and the lower thighs are yellowish. Unlike more conspicuously patterned leafbirds, its face lacks the prominent black throat mask found in some other species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Leafbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Surigao del Sur, and North Cotabato. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Philippine Leafbird inhabits forest; historical Philippine accounts also recorded breeding in June (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

Breeding males show a golden crown, dark streaked back and tawny underparts; females retain a streaked brown head (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Golden-headed Cisticola has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Lake Lanao, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range, Mount Nacolod, and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Golden-headed Cisticola is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

A small warbler with dark-streaked buff upperparts, rufous rump and pale underside with buff flanks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Zitting Cisticola is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Zitting Cisticola usually keeps low in long grass; territorial males circle and hover in display flights during breeding (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Zitting Cisticola is associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, as well as agricultural land.

A minute, very short-tailed bird with olive-green upperparts, a conspicuous yellow eyebrow and bright yellow underparts. Long, slender, white-shafted feathers on the lower back and flanks extend toward or beyond the tail tip. The bill is fine and slightly downcurved. The original Leyte series included a paler bird, but the author could not establish whether this reflected sex or age (Amadon, 1962). The Visayan Miniature Babbler is documented on Samar and Leyte. Older Mindanao reports under a broader Micromacronus leytensis concept are now generally treated as M. sordidus (WBCP, 2025; Avibase, 2026). The Visayan Miniature Babbler occurs in lowland old-growth forest on Samar, moving in small groups through the forest canopy. These observations concern the Visayan species rather than the separate Mindanao Miniature Babbler (BirdLife International, 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: The Mindanao form shares the miniature babbler’s olive-green upperparts, yellow underside and elongated white-shafted back and flank feathers. In the historical comparative specimen treatment, the Mindanao form (then M. leytensis sordidus) was described as slightly larger and darker than the Leyte nominate form, with a reported wing measurement of about 47 mm against 41 mm in the Leyte type. Those measurements come from small historical samples and should not be treated as a field threshold (duPont, 1971). The Mindanao Miniature Babbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Mindanao Miniature Babbler uses montane evergreen forest, forest edge and vegetation from the understorey to the canopy, often moving in small groups (BirdForum Opus, n.d.).

records.p: The Grey-headed Tailorbird shows a slate-grey head and nape, a contrasting white patch around the ear, a black throat and pale grey upper breast. The back is olive-green and the belly is mostly whitish, with yellow-olive on the sides. Immatures have more extensive pale feathering around the throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-eared Tailorbird is recorded on Mindanao and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Lake Lanao, Lake Holon, and Zamboanga del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The White-eared Tailorbird is broadly associated with forests. Bourns and Worcester recorded breeding on Basilan during August (McGregor, 1909–1910).

This tailorbird has a rufous-chestnut forehead and lores adjoining a contrasting ashy-grey crown. The remaining upperparts are olive, while the throat and central underparts are whitish and the breast sides can carry faint grey streaking. McGregor also described a Basilan form with rufous extending farther over the crown, demonstrating within-complex geographic variation (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-fronted Tailorbird has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Rufous-fronted Tailorbird is broadly associated with forest edge, shrubland, and cultivated land.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 17.4 mm, wing length of 51.8 mm, tail length of 47.5 mm, and body mass of 9.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Black-headed Tailorbird is recorded on Mindanao, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Bega Watershed, Mount Matutum, Mount Mayo, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black-headed Tailorbird is broadly associated with forests.

The adult male Yellow-breasted Tailorbird has a black head, throat and central upper breast, sharply bordered by lemon-yellow on the sides of the breast and belly. It has an olive-green back with a russet rump and tail-coverts. In the original comparison with Orthotomus nigriceps, the black breast patch is confined to the center rather than extending broadly onto the sides (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Yellow-breasted Tailorbird is recorded on Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park, Mount Huraw, and Eastern Samar. On Leyte, records include Lake Danao, Mount Lobi Range, and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Yellow-breasted Tailorbird uses forest vegetation along streams, with historical breeding observations in August (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

McGregor described this Philippine crow as predominantly black, with greenish to purplish sheen on the wings and body, a stout bill and a rounded tail. Those features recognize a crow but do not independently establish the identity of every black corvid at a distance. Historical specimens were placed under Corone philippina before the modern Corvus combination (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Jungle Crow has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Jungle Crow is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats, shrubland, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. The Clements 2024 checklist split Philippine Jungle Crow from the wider Corvus macrorhynchos treatment, citing distinctions involving size, shape and vocalizations among forms. Historical Philippine records under C. macrorhynchos need assessment before reassignment to C. philippinus, especially when they do not preserve identifying subspecies or specimen information (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2024).

The Samar Crow is an all-black crow with dark plumage, bill and feet. In the original comparison it was smaller than the crow then called Corvus pusillus, with a relatively short, deep bill. These comparative proportions were reported from a limited historical specimen series (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Samar Crow is recorded on Samar and Mindanao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Samar Crow has been observed on wooded hills, with older accounts describing it as shy. The working checklist also includes shrubland, open ground and modified habitats among its broad categories (McGregor, 1909–1910). The 2024 eBird taxonomy recognizes Samar Crow as separate from the formerly broad Slender-billed Crow complex (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2024).

Mann’s taxonomic treatment describes the nominate Dicaeum aeruginosum aeruginosum as olive-green above, greener on the rump, and whitish below with conspicuous brown breast streaks and a stout bill. This is a subspecies-level literature diagnosis, not a measured character range for every Philippine population (Mann, 2002). The Striped Flowerpecker has historical records from Mindanao, including the Mount Matutum area. Under the current Clements treatment, the Philippine taxon is included within Pachyglossa agilis, so this entry overlaps with that species account (GBIF.org, 2026; Avibase, 2026). The Striped Flowerpecker is broadly associated with forests.

In the species comparison published by Mann, adults of Dicaeum australe have a grey throat and upper breast, no broad black transverse breast band, and a narrow red stripe down the middle of an otherwise grey underside. The bill is broader, deeper and less strongly curved than that of D. haematostictum, which has a white throat and thick black breast band (Mann, 2002). The Red-keeled Flowerpecker is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Red-keeled Flowerpecker is broadly associated with forests.

The male Bicolored Flowerpecker has nearly black upperparts with a faint metallic blue sheen and a sharply contrasting white underside, including the underwing coverts. Early descriptions also record a dark bill and legs and a red iris (McGregor, 1909–1910, reporting Bourns and Worcester). Females and immature birds should not be assigned the same pattern without further comparison. The Bicolored Flowerpecker has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Bicolored Flowerpecker is broadly associated with forests.

The Buzzing Flowerpecker varies geographically. Birds assigned to the western Mindanao–Sulu hypoleucum group have strongly contrasting blackish upperparts and white underparts in males, with duller brown-backed females. The eastern Mindanao–Samar pontifex group is less contrasting, with dark olive upperparts and greyish underparts in both sexes. A genomic study recovered three regional lineages but documented gene flow, so these plumage groups are useful comparisons rather than separate species diagnoses (DeRaad et al., 2025). The Buzzing Flowerpecker is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Buzzing Flowerpecker has been recorded in deep forest and occasionally in coconut groves (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Males are recognized by the brightly coloured flame-orange to red crown, contrasting with the darker head and upperparts. The Philippine Eagle Foundation specimen exhibit documents that crown colour in this Mindanao flowerpecker. The species was formerly included with the Yellow-crowned Flowerpecker, D. anthonyi, of Luzon, but is treated separately in the 2023 Clements taxonomy (Philippine Eagle Foundation, 2022; Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2023). The Flame-crowned Flowerpecker is recorded from the mountains of Mindanao, including Mount Kampalili, Mount Melibengoy and Mount Malindang. Historical western Mindanao records were published under the subspecies name masawan (Manuel & Gilliard, 1953; Pitogo et al., 2024; Avibase, 2026). The Flame-crowned Flowerpecker inhabits montane forest on Mindanao, including eastern mountain ranges and the Mount Malindang region (Avibase, 2026). Manuel and Gilliard published the replacement name Dicaeum kampalili in 1953 for a flowerpecker named from Mount Kampalili, Mindanao (Manuel & Gilliard, 1953).

records.p: In the older Philippine descriptions, male Fire-throated Flowerpeckers have shining greenish upperparts, a red throat and upper breast, paler lower underparts and yellow undertail coverts. Mindanao birds described under the historical name Dicaeum apo were compared with Luzon D. luzoniense as having greener-black sides of the head and brighter yellow undertail feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). These comparisons refer to historical taxonomic forms and should not be treated as universal differences within the present D. luzoniense concept. The Fire-throated Flowerpecker is recorded in montane Mindanao, including the Mount Apo, Kitanglad, Malindang and Hilong-Hilong areas. A historically described subspecies is also known from Samar, and some older records use the pre-split name Dicaeum ignipectus (Avibase, 2026; DENR-PAWB, 2004). The Fire-throated Flowerpecker is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 9.4 mm, wing length of 46.8 mm, tail length of 24.6 mm, and body mass of 5.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Olive-capped Flowerpecker combines a greenish-yellow crown and nape with dark lores and a slim dark line through the eye. In McGregor’s specimens the mantle was brownish, upper breast grey, lower underparts pale and the flanks and undertail region distinctly yellow. The apparent prominence of the eye-line and grey breast varies with viewing angle and age (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Olive-capped Flowerpecker has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Olive-capped Flowerpecker is broadly associated with forests.

The Pygmy Flowerpecker is exceptionally small, with a short, fine bill. Adult males have a dark olive upperbody with a greenish gloss, white central throat and small white pectoral tufts, and pale underparts washed or mottled grey. Females are greyer around the head, with an olive back and subtler pale eyebrow and eye ring. Geographic forms vary in rump coloration and dorsal sheen (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Pygmy Flowerpecker has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Pygmy Flowerpecker uses deep woodland, with historical breeding records on Samar (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Males have slate-blue upperparts, an orange patch on the back and a bright orange-to-yellow belly; females are olive-brown with yellow below (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Orange-bellied Flowerpecker has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). Feeds on small fruit, nectar, pollen and tiny invertebrates, often among canopy foliage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

An olive-brown flowerpecker with pale, dark-streaked underparts, a stout dark bill and reddish-orange eyes (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Thick-billed Flowerpecker is recorded on Mindanao under the Clements treatment, which includes Philippine populations formerly separated as Dicaeum aeruginosum. Its Mindanao occurrence overlaps with the book’s historical Striped Flowerpecker account (Avibase, 2026; DENR-PAWB, 2004). The Thick-billed Flowerpecker is associated with forests. The Thick-billed Flowerpecker feeds in middle and upper vegetation on small fruits, mistletoes, flowers and insects; frequently jerks its tail sideways (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Olive-backed Flowerpecker has bright olive-green upperparts and wings edged with olive, contrasting with smoky grey underparts. A white line extends through the chin and centre of the lower body; the flanks bear white streaks. Females were described as similar, though generally greyer below (McGregor, 1909–1910, under Prionochilus olivaceus). The Olive-backed Flowerpecker is recorded from Mindanao and has a historical breeding report from Basilan under the former name Prionochilus olivaceus (McGregor, 1909–1910; Lepage, 2026; GBIF.org, 2026). The Olive-backed Flowerpecker feeds on fruits and seeds in forest and secondary growth; breeding was historically recorded on Basilan (McGregor, 1909–1910). The present Pachyglossa combination reflects a reassignment from older usage of Prionochilus olivaceus in some bird lists. Literature and museum records under the earlier combination require name-concept matching before their distribution or morphology is interpreted (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 2024).

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Dicaeum proprium: culmen 10.3 mm, wing 57.8 mm, tarsus 13.9 mm and body mass 10.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Whiskered Flowerpecker is recorded from southeastern Mindanao, including the Mount Mayo area of Davao Oriental (Ripley & Rabor, 1966; Avibase, 2026). The Whiskered Flowerpecker is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: This dark drongo has an unusually long, slender, gently downcurved bill. The tips of the outer tail feathers curve upward and inward, helping distinguish it from other drongos when the tail is seen clearly (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Under the current treatment of the drongo complex, Hair-crested Drongo records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte and Bohol in older datasets require reassignment review, particularly against the Short-tailed Drongo (D. striatus). The 2025 WBCP checklist places Philippine Hair-crested Drongo populations in the Sulu Archipelago rather than these Greater Mindanao islands (WBCP, 2025; Avibase, 2026). The Hair-crested Drongo is broadly associated with forests.

Velvety blue-black plumage, shiny scaly crown and steel-blue throat spangles characterize the southern drongo (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Short-tailed Drongo is recognized from Mindanao and Basilan as the nominate subspecies striatus, with the subspecies samarensis on Samar, Leyte and Bohol. The type locality of D. striatus is Pasonanca near Zamboanga, Mindanao. Earlier records under D. hottentottus striatus or a broader Hair-crested Drongo treatment should be assigned to the modern species only where their subspecies or geographic origin is clear (Avibase, 2026). The Short-tailed Drongo is associated with forests. A documented Basilan suspended nest of plant fibers held three pale spotted eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 12.4 mm, wing length of 68.1 mm, tail length of 54.9 mm, and body mass of 14.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Yellow Bunting has been documented on Mindanao, including Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Yellow Bunting is broadly associated with forests and freshwater wetlands. McGregor described seasonal wear and replacement of male plumage, including changes in the dark streaking of the mantle (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Red-eared Parrotfinch has a green body, bright blue forehead and face, a red crescent across the ear-coverts and side of the neck, and a red rump above the darker tail. The bill is dark to black in adults. Females generally show smaller blue and red areas, while juveniles are greener, have a duller reddish rump and a paler bill. These age and sex characters are summarized in BirdForum’s species account (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Red-eared Parrotfinch is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Red-eared Parrotfinch is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Black head and breast, rich chestnut body, grey-blue bill and dark centre of belly distinguish adults (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Chestnut Munia has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Chestnut Munia is associated with forests. The Chestnut Munia feeds on grass seeds from stems and the ground, often in flocks with other munias (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The White-bellied Munia is a small heavy-billed finch with brown upperparts, a black face and throat merging into the brown crown and back, and a striking clean white belly. The dark throat-to-white-belly contrast helps separate adults from more extensively chestnut or patterned munias. Young birds and worn plumages may require additional comparisons (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.). The White-bellied Munia has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The White-bellied Munia is broadly associated with forests.

r.short: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.

records.p: White underparts bear prominent dark scale-like markings, contrasting with brown upperparts; juveniles lack clear scales (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Scaly-breasted Munia has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Busa Mountain Range, and Sarangani. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Scaly-breasted Munia is associated with forests. The Scaly-breasted Munia feeds socially by climbing seed-bearing grasses and can join mixed-species munia groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A black crown, sharply white cheek patches, thick pink bill and gray upperparts make this finch conspicuous (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Java Sparrow has been reported as an introduced bird on the Zamboanga Peninsula of Mindanao. The published field record documents local occurrence but does not establish wider naturalized distribution (Paguntalan et al., 2011; Lepage, 2026). The Java Sparrow uses open and cultivated landscapes around settlements and rice fields. Flocks feed on seeds and grains, and birds may nest in tree cavities or buildings. Free-living Philippine populations include introduced or escaped birds (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, n.d.).

The smaller Samar broadbill has a purple-brown back, black face, chestnut tail, and white-striped wing (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Visayan Broadbill has records from Samar and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Mount Capotoan. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Visayan Broadbill is broadly associated with forests. A genomic study found that Bohol specimens formed a genetic group distinct from those from Samar and Leyte (Campillo et al., 2020). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A broad blue eye wattle, purple crown, gray back and yellow-and-white wingband mark adult males (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Wattled Broadbill has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Wattled Broadbill forages in small forest flocks, sometimes striking captured insects against branches before eating them (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 11.2 mm, wing length of 67 mm, tail length of 54 mm, and body mass of 12 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Mindanao Serin occurs in the mountains of Mindanao, with records from the Mount Kitanglad and Mount Apo regions. Earlier publications treated it as a subspecies of Chrysocorythus estherae (Ripley & Rabor, 1961; Avibase, 2026). The Mindanao Serin is broadly associated with forests, grasslands and other open habitats.

records.p: A compact, thick-billed bullfinch with a dark glossy crown, a conspicuously white cheek patch, dark flight feathers, a white rump and warm brown back and underparts. The inner secondaries may show a narrow orange-red edge in adult males, more yellow-orange in females. Historical Mindanao birds were separated as Pyrrhula steerei from northern P. leucogenys by a smaller, darker bill, browner body and a tendency toward a paler centre of the abdomen. These are population-level historic descriptions within the composite name used here, not a demonstrated diagnostic threshold for all Mindanao birds (Mearns, 1909, reproduced in McGregor, 1910). The White-cheeked Bullfinch has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, North Cotabato, and Davao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-cheeked Bullfinch is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 13.9 mm, wing length of 77 mm, tail length of 67 mm, and body mass of 19 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

Glossy blue-black upperparts contrast with a rufous rump; pale underparts show dark streaking, and the tail is deeply forked (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eastern Red-rumped Swallow has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Holon, Misamis Oriental, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Red-rumped Swallow is associated with forests, grasslands and other open areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. The Eastern Red-rumped Swallow forages in the air with a slow, buoyant flight and often accompanies other swallows (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Blue-black upperparts contrast with an entirely white rump, face and belly; the tail is only slightly forked (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian House-Martin is recorded from Mindanao (Lepage, 2026). The Asian House Martin catches flying insects in flocks above open ground and forest edges (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The blue-black upperparts, rufous forehead and throat, and shallowly forked tail distinguish this swallow; it lacks the complete dark breast band of Barn Swallow (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pacific Swallow is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). Takes flying insects on swift aerial circuits, often low over open ground; may roost with Barn Swallows (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). McGregor described mud-cup nests fixed under buildings or against rock; three incubated eggs were collected on Bohol in July (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A deeply forked tail and complete dark breast-band separate it from Pacific Swallow (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Glossy blue-black upperparts, a chestnut forehead and throat, a dark breast band and pale underparts mark adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Barn Swallow is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and North Cotabato. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod, Lake Danao, and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Barn Swallow catches flying insects in sustained low swooping flight over open terrain (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Barn Swallow is associated with grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas.

The Philippine Fairy-bluebird has a heavy dark face, lores, throat and upper breast contrasted with glossy royal-blue crown feathers and deep indigo-blue back and underparts. Its wings combine black and blue, the eyes are reddish, and the tail is mainly blue with a dark central area. The degree of dark versus indigo upperbody plumage varies among named subspecies. These details are compiled in the species-level BirdForum account and require confirmation against a specimen-based regional treatment (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Philippine Fairy-bluebird has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat and Siargao. Mindanao reports include the Mount Apo and Mount Hilong-Hilong regions, the Busa Mountain Range and historical observations from the Zamboanga area (Lint & Stott, 1948; GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Fairy-bluebird is broadly associated with forests.

r.full: Lint, K. C., & Stott, K., Jr. (1948). Notes on birds of the Philippines. The Auk, 65(1), 41–46. https://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v065n01/p0041-p0046.pdf

records.p: The brown upperparts and dark eye-mask contrast with a pale lower body (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Brown Shrike has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Brown Shrike is associated with forests. The Brown Shrike hunts from exposed perches and returns to cover after taking insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A large, long-tailed shrike with a black eye-mask, grey head, warm rufous flanks and black wings and tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Long-tailed Shrike has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Long-tailed Shrike is associated with grasslands and other open areas, shrublands, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. The Long-tailed Shrike hunts insects and small vertebrates from conspicuous lookout perches (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A slate-gray crown with a black eye mask and an evenly barred chestnut mantle create the characteristic tiger pattern (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Tiger Shrike has been documented in the Bega Watershed of Agusan del Sur, northeastern Mindanao (Calimpong & Nuñeza, 2015). The Tiger Shrike takes insects, lizards, small birds and rodents in wooded edges and secondary growth (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Tiger Shrike is associated with forests.

records.p: A stout hooked bill, gray upperparts, broad dark facial mask and pale underparts characterize adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mountain Shrike has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mountain Shrike is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Tawny Grassbird has a dull rufous-brown crown marked by diffuse dark shaft streaks, an off-white or grey-brown supercilium and a pale throat and belly. Adults of both sexes have similar plumage, although their measurements overlap rather than being identical. Juveniles show shorter dark crown streaks and a less defined buff supercilium (Australian Bird Study Association, n.d.). The Tawny Grassbird has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Tawny Grassbird is associated with forests habitats and caves and karst landscapes.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Locustella fasciolata: culmen 20.5 mm, wing 75.5 mm, tarsus 25.5 mm and body mass 27.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Gray’s Grasshopper Warbler has been recorded on Mindanao (Lepage, 2026). The Gray's Grasshopper Warbler is broadly associated with shrubland and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Locustella ochotensis: culmen 16.2 mm, wing 69.5 mm, tarsus 24.4 mm and body mass 18.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Middendorff's Grasshopper Warbler has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Surigao del Sur, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Middendorff's Grasshopper Warbler is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as shrubland.

The Mindanao form, Locustella caudata unicolor, was originally described as Pseudotharrhaleus unicolor. In the historical female specimen the upperparts were deep rufous-brown, and the underside was brown tinged with olive, with a paler, buff-washed upper throat. The tail was about 75 mm, shorter than the approximately 85–88 mm tails reported for the nominate Luzon form in the same early treatment (McGregor, 1909–1910). This comparison concerns the recorded forms and does not replace vocal or modern population-level diagnosis (Avibase, 2026). The Long-tailed Bush Warbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, Mount Talomo, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Long-tailed Bush Warbler is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as shrubland. The Mt. Melibengoy bird inventory flags its local long-tailed grasshopper warbler population as deserving targeted comparative work, without proposing a formal taxonomic change (Pitogo et al., 2024).

A small skulking warbler marked with narrow dark streaks on the crown, mantle, underside and undertail-coverts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Lanceolated Warbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan del Sur and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). Forages on or near the ground within grass and low scrub, often remaining concealed when approached (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A long tapered tail and large size distinguish this grassbird, with brown crown and strongly streaked dorsal plumage (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Striated Grassbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Striated Grassbird is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

Males have bright blue upperparts and breast, a black nuchal tuft and dark breast band; females are duller blue-grey and brown (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black-naped Monarch has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). Takes small insects with short sorties through the forest and forest edge (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The male Celestial Monarch has intense blue upperparts, throat and breast, a lighter bluish lower back and wings, a paler whitish belly tinged with blue, and a lilac-blue cheek area. A greenish-yellow bare eye ring and a long crest curving back over the crown are distinctive at close range. The female is generally less intensely blue and has a shorter crest (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Celestial Monarch has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Celestial Monarch is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.8 mm, wing length of 71 mm, tail length of 66.5 mm, and body mass of 13.6 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

Adult male Short-crested Monarchs have a rich blue head and upperbody, a dark facial mask edged with brighter blue, a prominent cobalt-blue patch of bare skin around the eye, and a raised or elongated crest. Females are duller, with reduced crest and blue facial contrasts. The illustrated Mindanao form is identified in the source as agusanae, so color differences between geographic forms should not be ignored (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Short-crested Monarch has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Mount Capotoan (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Short-crested Monarch has historical forest records from Samar. More recent surveys at Hijo Forest listed it historically but did not confirm its presence and noted possible confusion with the Black-naped Monarch (McGregor, 1909–1910; Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Males are largely black with a purple-glossed back, whitish belly and greatly elongated tail streamers; females have shorter tails and brown-toned plumage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Black Paradise Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Black Paradise Flycatcher catches insects in short flights from perches, often high in trees. The regional working checklist lists forests as well as coastal and intertidal habitats (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Rufous Paradise-flycatcher has predominantly warm rufous upperparts, including the flight feathers and tail, with a contrasting darker face and paler underbody in some ages and sexes. Tail length and ornamentation may differ by sex and maturity, and no single tail character should be used without comparison to the locally relevant Terpsiphone. This account is a preliminary external description from the BirdForum species synopsis (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Rufous Paradise Flycatcher has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Rufous Paradise Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests.

Strong dark streaks cover the back, breast and flanks; breeding adults have a pink-red throat and face, usually reduced or absent in nonbreeding birds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-throated Pipit has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-throated Pipit walks over open ground, picking insects and occasionally seeds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-throated Pipit is associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open areas, as well as agricultural land.

The Pechora Pipit has bold contrasting pale and dark stripes along the sides of its back, prominent dark streaks across the breast and flanks, pale pinkish legs and a relatively large, pale-based bill. Its white-tipped wing-coverts and the projection of the primary feathers beyond the tertials are helpful distinctions from other brown pipits (Carey and Pang, 2024). The Pechora Pipit has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, North Cotabato, and South Cotabato. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Pechora Pipit is associated with grasslands and other open areas, shrublands, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. Historical accounts describe migrants skulking alone on forested ground rather than gathering in flocks (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Olive-toned upperparts, broad pale eyebrow edged dark and bold breast streaking distinguish it from the more open-country Red-throated Pipit (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Olive-backed Pipit has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Olive-backed Pipit feeds on the ground close to shrubs or trees and often flies into woody cover when disturbed (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Olive-backed Pipit is associated with forests.

A pale-bellied pipit with streaked grey-brown upperparts, slender bill and relatively long legs and tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Paddyfield Pipit is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, South Cotabato, and Davao del Sur. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Paddyfield Pipit is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats, shrublands, agricultural landscapes, built-up and disturbed areas. Its flight is comparatively fluttering, and it rarely hovers before landing (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A long-tailed wagtail with grey upperparts and a yellow vent; males in breeding plumage acquire a dark throat and brighter yellow underside (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Grey Wagtail is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Grey Wagtail forages along streams for aquatic invertebrates, continually pumping its exceptionally long tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Grey Wagtail is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 16.2 mm, wing length of 85.5 mm, tail length of 82.8 mm, and body mass of 19.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Citrine Wagtail has been documented on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Citrine Wagtail is broadly associated with rivers and streams and coastal and intertidal habitats.

AVONET lists a culmen length of 15.9 mm, wing length of 78.8 mm, tail length of 66.5 mm, and body mass of 18.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Eastern Yellow Wagtail is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, and Surigao del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Eastern Yellow Wagtail is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

Philippine shortwings have compact bodies, short wings and tail, and a relatively long, slender tarsus. In McGregor’s historical treatments, males are predominantly dark slate to blackish and have a partly concealed white eyebrow patch, while females may have a rusty-brown head, face and throat contrasting with slaty body plumage. The old name B. poliogyna referred specifically to northern populations; Mindanao birds were described separately as B. mindanensis and B. malindangensis. Therefore this description indicates a complex under the modern broad Philippine Shortwing name and does not establish one uniform set of characters for all populations (McGregor, 1910). The Philippine Shortwing has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Shortwing is broadly associated with montane habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 15.5 mm, wing length of 64.3 mm, tail length of 55.2 mm, and body mass of 17.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The male Philippine Magpie-Robin has a glossy blue-black head, upperparts, throat and breast, a sharply contrasting white lower belly, and white inner wing-coverts. The female is duller, with ash-grey across the forehead, throat and breast. Young birds are more sooty above and show pale spotting on the dark breast (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Magpie-Robin has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Lake Danao on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Magpie-Robin is broadly associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, shrubland, and cultivated land.

The Philippine Jungle Flycatcher was described under Rhinomyias ruficauda as olive-brown above, with a conspicuous ferruginous or rufous tail and relatively pale grey face. The centre of the underparts is whitish, while females were described as duller around the face. Tail colour and underpart tone provide initial recognition characters but should be compared with similar forest flycatchers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Jungle Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Philippine Jungle Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests.

The male Mangrove Blue Flycatcher has blue upperparts and a rich orange-rufous throat and belly, grading to a whitish vent. The female is similar but shows white around the lores and below the eye, as well as on the chin. A regional comparison distinguishes the widespread taxon from the Chinese Blue Flycatcher by orange-rufous extending farther down the underparts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Philippine subspecific variation requires local comparison. The Mangrove Blue Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Lumot, Agusan del Norte, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mangrove Blue Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests.

The adult Turquoise Flycatcher has bluish-green (verditer) upperparts and upper breast, darker wings and tail with blue-edged feathers, and a contrasting paler lower belly. In the Mindanao population historically called Stoparola panayensis nigriloris (later Eumyias nigriloris), the lores were described as wholly dark to the feather tips, and the lower abdomen and undertail as creamy buff, in contrast to the paler lores and more whitish undertail of nominate Panay birds. The original distinction was based on specimens under older taxonomic limits and should not be used uncritically as a field key across the modern species range (Hartert, 1904, reproduced in McGregor, 1910). The Turquoise Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Turquoise Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests.

In the historical description under Muscicapula basilanica, the male Little Slaty Flycatcher has dark slate-blue upperparts and head, pale underparts, and small concealed white patches on the nape. The female was described as predominantly brown with a more chestnut-coloured tail and whitish underparts. These markedly different plumages make sex important when comparing field observations (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Little Slaty Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Little Slaty Flycatcher has been recorded close to the forest floor on Mindanao and Basilan (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The Cryptic Flycatcher is a small, subdued flycatcher. In a documented Mindanao comparison, adults had a pale olive-brown band across the breast and grey to greyish-pink legs. A recently fledged bird showed warmer orange-buff around the face, upper breast and flanks, pale flesh-coloured legs, a very short, pointed tail and a chestnut wing-bar formed by the greater coverts (Collins, 2016). These age-related characters are most useful when considered together; the juvenile plumage should not be treated as the appearance of all adults. The Cryptic Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Mount Hamiguitan Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Mount Pasian, and Agusan del Norte. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Cryptic Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests.

r.full: Collins, A. R. (2016). First description of a juvenile Cryptic Flycatcher Ficedula crypta. BirdingASIA, 26, 57–58. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/314258550_First_description_of_a_juvenile_Cryptic_Flycatcher_Ficedula_crypta

records.p: The Mindanao Mount Apo form, Ficedula luzoniensis montigena, was described as Muscicapula montigena. Adult males have dark slaty-blue upperparts, a white eyebrow reduced to small patches above the eyes, ochraceous underparts with a pale belly, and reddish-brown tail feathers. The historical female specimens were similarly patterned but had a more olive-washed back and buff around the eye (McGregor, 1909–1910). These are characters of the recorded Mindanao form, not a blanket description of every island subspecies (Avibase, 2026). The Bundok Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Bundok Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests and shrubland. The historical literature reports young birds collected in Benguet, Luzon, in July (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Adult males have dark upperparts, bright orange throat and breast, and a short pale eyebrow beginning behind the eye; females are greyer and duller (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Mugimaki Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Mugimaki Flycatcher generally forages alone for insects at low and middle levels of woodland (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adult males have a yellow eyebrow and a dark upper body contrasting with yellow underside; females are browner and show variable dark markings on the throat (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Narcissus Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Mount Matutum, and Lituban–Quipit Watershed. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Narcissus Flycatcher is associated with forests. Makes short flycatching flights for insects, often in the middle levels of trees (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The male Little Pied Flycatcher has a compact black-and-white pattern, with dark upperparts, pale underparts and a distinct white brow and wing markings. Females are principally brown above and pale below, lacking the male’s stark contrast. Identification should consider sex and age, because the dull females can resemble other Ficedula species; the regional form and vocalizations are important for confirmation (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Little Pied Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Balatukan, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Little Pied Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests. Breeding was reported in Benguet, northern Luzon, in an early account of this forest flycatcher (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Males have a deep blue back, black face and flanks, and white underparts; females are grey-brown with bluish wings and tail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Siberian Blue Robin was historically listed from Mindanao under the former name Luscinia cyane bochaiensis. Its current regional occurrence has not been independently confirmed (DENR-PAWB, 2004; Avibase, 2026). The Siberian Blue Robin runs and hops through damp forest leaf litter, twitches its tail and sometimes bathes in streams (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Siberian Blue Robin is associated with forests as well as rivers and streams.

The original adult male was described with deep brown upperparts, a nearly black tail, slate-grey cheeks and underparts, a conspicuous white chin and throat, and tawny-olive undertail coverts. The exceptionally long tarsi and soft, elongated rump feathers were also noted. These features describe the original male specimen, not measured variation in females or a modern comparative key (Mearns, 1905, as reproduced by McGregor, 1910). The Bagobo Babbler has been documented on Mindanao, including Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Lanao, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Bagobo Babbler is broadly associated with forests.

AVONET lists comparative values under the older name Cyanecula svecica: culmen 15.1 mm, wing 73.1 mm, tarsus 26.3 mm and body mass 17.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Bluethroat has been reported from Mindanao as a rare visitor (Lepage, 2026). The Bluethroat is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands and shrubland.

Adult males of the philippensis form are blue above and on the upper breast, contrasting with chestnut lower underparts; females show scaly brown-grey plumage (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Blue Rock Thrush has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, Agusan del Norte, and Agusan del Sur. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Blue Rock Thrush is associated with settlements and disturbed habitats. Scans for prey from a rock or other low vantage point, then drops to the ground to capture it (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A plain ashy-brown flycatcher with whitish underside, pale lores and a notably pale base to the lower mandible (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Asian Brown Flycatcher is included on current Mindanao bird checklists as a migratory visitor. Its treatment has changed with the separation of related brown flycatchers, including M. williamsoni; earlier Philippine observations identified only as a broad brown-flycatcher complex should therefore be checked against the diagnostic basis and migration date before assigning them to M. dauurica sensu stricto (Avibase, 2026). The Asian Brown Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests and coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Grey-streaked Flycatcher is grey-brown above and white below, with sharply defined dark streaks across the breast and flanks. It shows a pale narrow eye-ring, a whitish stripe below the moustachial line and a relatively long primary projection. Sexes look similar; first-winter birds may show pale tips to the greater coverts and fringed tertials (Diskin and Pang, 2023). The Grey-streaked Flycatcher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Lobi Range on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Grey-streaked Flycatcher is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

Adult male Pied Bushchats are predominantly black, broken by a conspicuous white wing patch and white vent. Females are dark brown, with a warmer reddish-brown rump and lower body and no obvious pale eyebrow. Female Siberian Stonechats can resemble them, but typically show pale markings on the collar or wing absent in female Pied Bushchats. Plumage is strongly sex-dependent (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird, n.d.). The Pied Bush Chat is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Mount Nacolod on Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Pied Bush Chat is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats and cultivated land.

records.p: McGregor described a female of this jungle flycatcher under Rhinomyias goodfellowi as dark slate-grey to blackish on the head and back, with a narrow pale band across the forehead above the lores, white central underparts and buff-coloured flanks. This is a documented female specimen description, not a confirmed account of male or juvenile appearance (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Slaty-backed Jungle Flycatcher has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Davao del Sur, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Slaty-backed Jungle Flycatcher is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 18.2 mm, wing length of 85.5 mm, tail length of 68.2 mm, and body mass of 31.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The male Handsome Sunbird has an iridescent green forecrown, dark olive-green nape, yellow lower back and bright yellow breast. A narrow iridescent malar stripe and purplish ear patch contrast with a slim crimson margin beside the throat. The female has a yellow rump against a greener back. Mann separated this form from A. shelleyi, which has a crimson nape and red lower back (Mann, 2002). The Handsome Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Handsome Sunbird is broadly associated with forests and shrubland. A nest record from near Paranas, Samar, on 19 July 1895 yielded three freshly laid, pinkish-white eggs with reddish markings (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 20.1 mm, wing length of 49.4 mm, tail length of 40.7 mm, and body mass of 7.1 g (Tobias et al., 2022). The Apo Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, and North Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Apo Sunbird is associated with high-elevation montane forests of Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

The male Lina’s Sunbird has a dark greyish head and metallic blue highlights, a pale yellow throat stripe and upper breast, and a contrasting reddish-orange breast patch. The tail is elongated, with pale tips on its graduated feathers. Females are duller and lack the strong metallic markings (Philippine Red List Committee, n.d.; Philippine Eagle Foundation, 2022). The Lina's Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Tagubud, Mount Pasian, Davao del Norte, and Davao de Oro (GBIF.org, 2026). The Lina's Sunbird is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 22.5 mm, wing length of 52 mm, tail length of 40.1 mm, and body mass of 7.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: The Grey-hooded Sunbird is recognizable by its grey head and neck, which contrast with the pale belly and olive-green back and wings. Males have small metallic olive-green patches on the forehead and ear region that are absent in females (Philippine Red List Committee, n.d.). The Grey-hooded Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Hilong-Hilong, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Grey-hooded Sunbird is broadly associated with forests. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: Male Metallic-winged Sunbirds show a metallic blue forehead and green or blue-glossed wing-coverts against olive upperparts, a bright yellow rump and yellow lower underparts. The chest has a conspicuous red or scarlet area; females lack the bright metallic and scarlet male pattern and are more olive-brown above and yellow below. The sexes should therefore be compared separately (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Metallic-winged Sunbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Dinagat, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Metallic-winged Sunbird is broadly associated with forests. Three slightly incubated eggs were collected near Paranas, Samar, on 26 July 1896; the shells had pinkish-gray mottling (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A small sunbird with a distinctly decurved bill, gray head, olive upperparts, yellow rump and yellow belly. Adult males have a narrow yellow stripe on the throat bordered by darker gray, a bluish-green tail and an orange patch near the front of the shoulder; females show a paler gray throat and faint streaking across the breast. The yellow rather than white belly is a useful distinction from the Gray-hooded Sunbird. Sex and age should be considered when applying plumage characters, and field identification is stronger when supported by photographs or vocalizations (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, eBird). The Tboli Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Melibengoy, Mount Matutum, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Tboli Sunbird is broadly associated with forests. The Mount Melibengoy report recognizes the Tboli sunbird as a distinct species, while acknowledging its original description as a form of the Apo sunbird group. It associates the named form with high-elevation forest in Mt. Melibengoy, Mt. Busa and nearby Mt. Matutum (Pitogo et al., 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Males have a notably grey throat above pale lower underparts and small light lemon-yellow tufts at the sides of the breast. McGregor contrasted this with the more yellow-bellied appearance of the similar Brown-throated Sunbird, A. chlorigaster. Females were described as duller, with greenish upperparts, so male throat colour should not be applied uncritically to all birds (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Grey-throated Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Misamis Oriental, and Surigao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Grey-throated Sunbird is broadly associated with forests, cultivated land, and coastal and intertidal habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 18.9 mm, wing length of 61 mm, tail length of 36.2 mm, and body mass of 15 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Males show a brown face and throat, iridescent green back, purple shoulder and yellow underside; females are mostly olive-brown and yellow (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Brown-throated Sunbird is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Apo Natural Park, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, and Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Brown-throated Sunbird is associated with settlements and disturbed habitats. Visits flowers alone or in pairs, sometimes driving other birds away from a nectar source (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A long-billed spiderhunter with partly bare facial skin. Collar, Halley and Hutchinson (2026) distinguish the Samar–Leyte–Biliran population formerly called A. c. philippinensis by a bare pinkish-yellow band continuing from the lores over the forehead, paler lores, an entirely whitish line at the bill commissure, and a shorter tail. By contrast, eastern Mindanao A. c. clarae and western Mindanao/Basilan birds formerly termed A. c. malindangensis show dark lores and a sharply two-coloured commissural line; the study found no clear difference between those two Mindanao forms. The authors propose species rank for A. philippinensis. Because this edition retains the pre-revision composite account, these characters distinguish its regional forms rather than confirm a single species across all listed islands. The Naked-faced Spiderhunter has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Northern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Naked-faced Spiderhunter is broadly associated with forests, shrubland, and cultivated land.

The Orange-tufted Spiderhunter has a long, downward-curved bill, olive-coloured upperparts, a muted greyish throat and breast and a bright yellow lower belly. McGregor described small orange-yellow tufts on the sides of the chest in males; the female did not show those tufts. A missing tuft therefore cannot by itself exclude a female of this species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Orange-tufted Spiderhunter has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Basilan, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Orange-tufted Spiderhunter is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 41.8 mm, wing length of 66.9 mm, tail length of 42 mm, and body mass of 11.8 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Garden Sunbird has olive-green upperparts and a slender, decurved bill. Adult males show a dark iridescent blue-black throat and upper breast above yellow underparts; females are yellow below, with a pale eyebrow and no dark iridescent throat patch. This description refers to the Philippine Garden Sunbird rather than the Australian sunbirds historically included under the broader name (Pranada, 2023). The Garden Sunbird has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Garden Sunbird is associated with forests, shrublands, agricultural areas, and coastal and intertidal habitats. Early observers described a woven, pendant pouch nest with a side entrance, using plant fibers and spider silk (McGregor, 1909–1910).
